To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the economic vote is a rational response to the economic conditions that voters observe.

1) The economic vote exists, but it is not as strong as some of its most vocal proponents claim; 2) the economic vote is not a simple, direct relationship between retrospective evaluations and the vote; 3) the economic vote depends on voters' perceptions of the economy and the political actors' responsibility for it; 4) the economic vote does not depend on the degree of economic change, but it does depend on the distribution of responsibility and contention over the economy; and

(i) the economic vote is a significant and robust phenomenon in western democracies, (ii) economic voting is a rational response to variation in economic outcomes, and (iii) rational retrospective economic voting is conditioned by the structure of political and economic institutions.
